Strava didn't transform running — but it proved remarkably effective at anchoring the habit for millions of practitioners, by making effort visible and social. Creative writing thrives on regularity and routine too. The question was simple: how do you transpose those mechanisms to a practice like writing?
As I built the first prototype, a second question came up: what does it mean to write in the age of LLMs? When anyone can generate text in seconds, what still makes writing valuable?
Both questions led to the same answer: practice. Writing has value because you show up and do the work. Inklyne is built on that idea.

Showing up matters more than being perfect. A few lines every day outweigh occasional marathon sessions. So: a distraction-free editor, session tracking, personal stats, and a social feed that makes your commitment visible to others.

AI is available for feedback, for structural questions, for the kind of editorial push you'd get from a thoughtful reader. But it cannot write a single line for you. The guardrails are intentional. If AI writes, we learn nothing, feel nothing.
This led to a feature I hadn't planned: session-based human authorship certification. Every session is timestamped and attributed. The act of writing becomes verifiable.
